label: Title
notes: Open by naming the chapter's central turn: curvature is no longer an informal bending picture but a quantity extracted from a Riemannian metric. The lecture will move from coordinates to invariant comparison, using the notebook artifacts as checks rather than as decorative illustrations.

label: Chapter Question
notes: Frame the guiding question as a chain of translations. The metric gives lengths, Christoffel symbols correct coordinate derivatives, curvature measures infinitesimal spreading, and comparison theorems convert those infinitesimal facts into triangle inequalities. Students should hear the whole chapter as one pipeline.

label: Metric In Coordinates
notes: Emphasize that the coordinate formula is not the geometry itself. The matrix g records how the coordinate grid should be measured at each point. The conformal model is useful because one scalar factor changes lengths while keeping angles visually recognizable.

label: Christoffel Correction
notes: The main conceptual point is that ordinary componentwise differentiation sees the moving coordinate frame as fixed. Christoffel symbols record how the frame changes. In the conformal test, every listed residual vanishes, so the symbolic computation agrees with the theoretical connection formula.

label: Constant Curvature Test
notes: Use this slide as the exact-computation anchor. The stereographic conformal factor produces Gaussian curvature k, and the residual K minus k is zero in the check file. This is where algebra, model geometry, and the visual wavefront artifact meet.

label: Covariant Derivative
notes: Explain the covariant derivative as the replacement for naive differentiation that respects the metric and the product rule. It is not an extra structure being chosen arbitrarily here; the Levi-Civita connection is the unique torsion-free metric-compatible correction.

label: Geodesic And Normal Curvature
notes: Separate intrinsic and extrinsic language carefully. Geodesic curvature is the tangential failure of a curve to be a surface geodesic. Normal curvature is what an ambient observer sees in the surface normal direction. The same drawn curve can carry both measurements.

label: Distance Circles
notes: Introduce S_k(r) as the ruler for polar spreading. In Euclidean space the circumference scale is r, on the sphere it grows like sin r, and in hyperbolic space it grows like sinh r. The checked Jacobi residual explains why these are the right functions.

label: HTML Lab
notes: Treat the linked lab as an inspection station. The slider changes k, and students should watch the same polar metric coefficient switch from compressed spherical spreading to flat spreading to hyperbolic expansion. The slide is not asking them to trust a picture.

label: Metric Distortion
notes: The local meaning of Gaussian curvature appears in how small metric circles and normal-coordinate distances deviate from flat expectations. Positive curvature makes nearby radial geodesics reconverge; negative curvature makes them separate faster. This is the bridge from formulas to comparison.

label: Jacobi And Rauch
notes: Present Jacobi fields as derivatives of a family of geodesics, not as mysterious vector fields. Rauch comparison says curvature bounds order the growth of these fields. That statement is the engine behind the later local and global triangle comparison results.

label: Model Triangle Residuals
notes: The residual plot gives a concrete sign test. For the fixed radial data in the check, positive curvature model sides fall below Euclidean values, while negative curvature model sides sit above them. This is the triangle-comparison intuition in numerical form.

label: Bridge Theorems
notes: Name the bridge without pretending the full global proof is contained in one slide. Cartan, Alexandrov, and Toponogov turn differential curvature control into metric triangle comparison under the right hypotheses. The local-to-global passage is powerful but hypothesis-sensitive.

label: Source Coverage
notes: Use the coverage map to orient students and to show provenance. The deck follows the assigned source span from coordinate computations through comparison theorems, while the notebook and artifacts supply original checks and visualizations rather than copied textbook material.

label: Break A Hypothesis
notes: This lab-style slide asks students to diagnose which assumption has been removed. If smoothness, metric compatibility, curvature bounds, or completeness disappears, the comparison conclusion can fail or become meaningless. The goal is to make theorem hypotheses feel operational.

label: Takeaways
notes: Close by returning to the pipeline. Coordinates give formulas, Christoffel symbols correct derivatives, curvature controls Jacobi spreading, and comparison theorems express those controls as metric inequalities. The checks are deliberately visible so students can audit the logic.
